stump noun

also tree stump, stock (of a tree), stub

classical

Verg. A. 12.208: scēptrum in silvīs īmō dē stirpe recīsum (Lewis & Short)
Cato Agr. 161.3: stirpēs fīent et intermorientur
Liv. 21.36.1

stirps, stirpis f.

noun, third declension

the stock of a tree: the bottom of the trunk with its roots, and so what is left in the ground when the tree is cut or broken off

Properly the lower part of the trunk together with the roots (Lewis & Short). Cato uses it of plants snapped off short, Livy of what sticks out of a rock face for a climber to hold. The other words name the trunk itself.

Other words

  • truncus, truncī m. — the trunk or bole of a tree, without regard to its branches

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 3.179 (Lewis & Short); Caes. BG 4.17 (Lewis & Short)

  • caudex (cōdex), caudicis m. — the trunk or stock of a tree; a block of wood

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Verg. G. 2.30 (Lewis & Short); Plin. NH 16.121 (Lewis & Short)

  • stīpes, stīpitis m. — a log, a post, a stake; a tree trunk

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Caes. BG 7.73 (Lewis & Short); Ov. Met. 8.451 (Lewis & Short)

Examples

  • nam sī dēfringēs, stirpēs fīent et intermorientur

    for if you break them off, they will turn into stumps and die offCato Agr. 161.3

  • manibusque retinēns virgulta ac stirpēs circā ēminentēs

    and holding on with his hands to the bushes and stumps that stuck out round aboutLiv. 21.36.1

  • quīn et caudicibus sectīs (mīrābile dictū) trūditur ē siccō rādīx oleāgina lignō

    why, even when the trunk has been cut up (wonderful to tell) an olive root pushes out of the dry woodVerg. G. 2.30–31

See also trunk, log, root.
